definition: The middle number when you line up all the values from smallest to largest.
example: Test scores: 3, 7, 9, 12, 100 — Median: 9 (Average: 26.2, dragged up by 100).
whyItMatters: The median ignores extreme values, so reports on things like income use it.

definition: A data point that sits far away from all the other numbers in a group.
example: In heights 142, 145, 147, 148, and 210 cm, 210 cm is the outlier.
whyItMatters: One outlier can skew an average or signal an important discovery.

definition: A number between 0 and 1 (or 0% to 100%) measuring how likely an event is.
example: Flipping a fair coin gives Heads with probability 0.5 (50%).
whyItMatters: Weather forecasts, sports analytics, and games all run on probability.

definition: When two things tend to move together—either up together or in opposite directions.
example: Ice cream sales and sunscreen sales both rise in summer.
whyItMatters: Two things moving together does not mean one caused the other!

definition: How many items or people you actually measure out of a much bigger group.
example: Asking 1,000 students instead of all 100,000 students in a city.
whyItMatters: Too small a sample can give a misleading result by pure luck.

definition: The sum of all values divided by how many values there are.
whyItMatters: Helps summarize a whole list with a single typical number.

definition: The value that appears most often in a data set.
example: In shoe sizes 36, 38, 38, 39, 41, the mode is 38.
whyItMatters: Stores use mode to know which sizes to stock the most.

definition: The difference between the largest and smallest numbers in a data set.
example: For temperatures 12°C to 27°C, the range is 27 - 12 = 15°C.
whyItMatters: Range shows how spread out the data is at a glance.

definition: A measure of how far numbers typically spread out from the average.
example: Test scores all near 85 have a tiny standard deviation; scores from 30 to 100 have a big one.
whyItMatters: Helps teachers and scientists tell consistent results from wildly mixed ones.

definition: The average of the squared distances from the mean.
example: Squaring deviations keeps negative and positive differences from canceling out.
whyItMatters: Variance is the building block behind standard deviation and risk models.

definition: A bar chart that groups numbers into ranges (bins) to show their frequency.
example: Counting how many students scored 60–70, 70–80, 80–90, and 90–100.
whyItMatters: Reveals the overall shape of data instantly.

definition: A chart using rectangular bars whose lengths match the size of each category.
example: Comparing favorite sports across a school class.
whyItMatters: Makes comparing separate categories clear and visual.

definition: A chart that connects data points with lines to show how something changes over time.
example: Tracking your height every birthday from age 5 to 11.
whyItMatters: Ideal for spotting trends, growth, or sudden drops.

definition: A graph of dots showing pairs of numbers to reveal patterns between two variables.
example: Plotting study hours on the x-axis against test scores on the y-axis.
whyItMatters: Helps spot correlations, clusters, and outliers.

definition: A circular chart divided into slices showing how a whole is split into parts.
example: Showing 50% sleep, 25% school, 25% free time.
whyItMatters: Quickly shows percentage shares of a single total.

definition: A compact chart showing minimum, quartiles, median, and maximum values.
example: Comparing reaction times across three video game controllers side by side.
whyItMatters: Packs five key summary numbers into one clean graphic.

definition: Values that split sorted data into four equal quarters (25% each).
example: The 2nd quartile is the median (50% mark).
whyItMatters: Used in school percentiles and medical growth charts.

definition: A score showing the percentage of values in a group that fall below yours.
example: Scoring in the 90th percentile means you beat 90% of test takers.
whyItMatters: Doctors and standardized tests use percentiles to compare fairly.

definition: The spread of the middle 50% of data (Q3 minus Q1).
example: Ignoring the top 25% and bottom 25% gives a sturdy measure of spread.
whyItMatters: Unlike total range, it is not ruined by one extreme outlier.

definition: A symmetric bell-shaped curve where most values cluster around the average.
example: Adult human heights follow a normal bell curve.
whyItMatters: Appears everywhere in biology, measurement errors, and test scores.

definition: Data whose distribution stretches out much farther on one side than the other.
example: House prices are right-skewed because a few mansions pull the tail high.
whyItMatters: When data is skewed, median is more honest than mean.

definition: The entire group of people, items, or events you want to learn about.
example: Every 11-year-old student in the country.
whyItMatters: Usually too huge to measure directly, so we take a sample instead.

definition: A sample where every member of the population has an equal chance of being picked.
example: Drawing names out of a well-shuffled hat.
whyItMatters: Prevents cherry-picking so results represent the whole group.

definition: When a survey picks a group that doesn't represent everyone fairly.
example: Asking only people at a skatepark if they like skateboarding.
whyItMatters: Biased samples produce completely wrong predictions.

definition: Focusing only on things that succeeded or survived while ignoring the ones that failed.
example: Assuming all old buildings were built better because the weak ones collapsed.
whyItMatters: Reminds us to look at missing data, not just visible winners.

definition: When one event directly makes another event happen.
example: Flipping a light switch causes the bulb to turn on.
whyItMatters: Statistics must test carefully to prove causation, not just correlation.

definition: A hidden third factor that influences both things you are comparing.
example: Summer heat causes both more ice cream sales and more sunburns.
whyItMatters: Spotting confounders stops false conclusions.

definition: A comparison group in an experiment that does not receive the treatment being tested.
example: Giving half the plants a new fertilizer and half plain water.
whyItMatters: Proves whether the treatment actually worked better than nothing.

definition: When people feel better just because they believe they received real medicine.
example: A sugar pill reducing headaches when the patient expects relief.
whyItMatters: Drug trials use placebos to measure real chemical effects.

definition: An experiment where neither the participants nor the researchers know who got the real treatment.
example: Numbered pill bottles decoded only after the trial ends.
whyItMatters: Eliminates accidental hints or biased scoring.

definition: A testable prediction or educated guess about how something works.
example: 'Plants watered with soda will grow slower than plants given plain water.'
whyItMatters: Every scientific experiment starts with a clear hypothesis.

definition: The default assumption that a test or treatment has no real effect.
example: Assuming a coin is fair (50/50) until data proves otherwise.
whyItMatters: Protects science from fooling itself with random luck.

definition: The chance of seeing results at least this extreme if nothing special is happening.
example: A p-value of 0.01 means a 1% chance the result was just luck.
whyItMatters: Helps scientists decide when an effect is real vs. coincidence.

definition: A range of values likely to contain the true population number.
example: A poll predicting 52% ± 3% means the true number is likely between 49% and 55%.
whyItMatters: Shows how precise an estimate really is.

definition: The plus-or-minus wiggle room around a survey result.
example: 54% with a ±4% margin of error.
whyItMatters: Bigger samples shrink the margin of error.

definition: As you repeat an experiment more times, the average result gets closer to the true probability.
example: Flipping a coin 10 times might give 70% heads; flipping 10,000 times gives ~50%.
whyItMatters: Explains why casinos and insurance companies are predictable long-term.

definition: The false belief that past random results change the odds of the next independent event.
example: Thinking a fair coin is 'due' for Tails after 5 Heads in a row.
whyItMatters: A coin has no memory—every flip is still 50/50.

definition: The long-run average outcome if you repeat a chance game many times.
example: Rolling a fair 6-sided die has an expected value of 3.5.
whyItMatters: Used to judge whether a bet, game, or investment is fair.

definition: Two events where the outcome of one does not affect the outcome of the other.
example: Rolling a 6 on a die and drawing an Ace from a deck.
whyItMatters: Lets you multiply probabilities cleanly.

definition: Events where the first outcome changes the odds of the second outcome.
example: Drawing an Ace from a deck and NOT putting it back before drawing again.
whyItMatters: Card games and raffle drawings work with dependent odds.

definition: The chance of event A happening given that event B already happened.
example: The chance of carrying an umbrella given that it is raining.
whyItMatters: Spam filters and medical tests rely on conditional probability.

definition: A formula for updating your belief about an event when new evidence arrives.
example: Updating the chance of rain when you suddenly see dark storm clouds.
whyItMatters: Powers medical diagnostics, search ranking, and self-driving cars.

definition: A test that wrongly says 'yes' when the real answer is 'no'.
example: A smoke alarm beeping because of burnt toast when there is no fire.
whyItMatters: Too many false positives make people ignore warnings.

definition: A test that wrongly says 'no' when the real answer is 'yes'.
example: A virus test missing an actual infection.
whyItMatters: Airport security and medical screenings work hard to minimize false negatives.

definition: Comparing two versions (A and B) with random users to see which performs better.
example: Testing a red button vs. a blue button on a website.
whyItMatters: Apps and websites use A/B tests daily to improve design.

definition: The straight line that best fits the trend through a scatter plot of points.
example: Drawing a trend line through height vs. age points.
whyItMatters: Helps predict future values from past data.

definition: An average where some items count more than others.
example: Final grade = 70% exams + 30% homework.
whyItMatters: Used in school grades, sports rankings, and stock indexes.

definition: An average calculated over a sliding window of recent data points.
example: A 7-day moving average of daily temperatures smooths out one weird day.
whyItMatters: Reveals real trends hidden inside noisy daily numbers.

definition: A table listing each item or range and how many times it occurred.
example: Counting how many cars of each color pass a corner in 10 minutes.
whyItMatters: First step in turning messy observations into clean charts.

definition: How often an outcome happens divided by the total number of trials.
example: Winning 12 out of 40 games gives a relative frequency of 0.3 (30%).
whyItMatters: Estimates real-world probability from experiments.

definition: A branching chart showing all possible sequences of outcomes.
example: Branching Heads/Tails for flip 1, then Heads/Tails for flip 2.
whyItMatters: Makes multi-step probability problems easy to count.

definition: The set of every single possible outcome of an experiment.
example: For a 6-sided die, the sample space is {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
whyItMatters: You must know all possibilities before calculating fair odds.

definition: How many standard deviations a value sits above or below the average.
example: A z-score of +2 means you are two standard deviations above average.
whyItMatters: Lets you compare scores from completely different tests.

definition: When a trend appears in separate groups but reverses when you combine the groups together.
example: A player has a higher batting average than another in both halves of a season, yet a lower overall average.
whyItMatters: Shows why splitting data by group size is crucial.

definition: In a room of just 23 people, there is over a 50% chance two people share a birthday.
example: 23 people form 253 pairs, creating 253 chances for a match.
whyItMatters: Our intuition often underestimates how fast pairs grow.

definition: A famous probability puzzle where switching doors doubles your chance of winning a prize.
example: 1/3 chance at first, 2/3 chance if you switch after a goat door is revealed.
whyItMatters: Shows how new information changes conditional odds.

definition: Another name for the normal distribution graph, shaped like a bell.
example: Most people are near the middle; very few are at the extreme ends.
whyItMatters: Commonly used in grading, biology, and manufacturing quality.

definition: A tight group of data points sitting close together on a graph.
example: Stars grouped into galaxies or customers with similar habits.
whyItMatters: Streaming apps use clustering to recommend music and movies.

definition: Data points collected in order at regular time intervals.
example: Hourly temperatures recorded all week.
whyItMatters: Used to forecast weather, traffic, and electricity demand.

definition: An unusual data point or pattern that breaks normal expectations.
example: A sudden midnight spike in website traffic.
whyItMatters: Banks use anomaly detection to spot stolen credit cards.

definition: Extreme measurements tend to be followed by ones closer to the average.
example: After scoring a lucky 100%, your next quiz is likely closer to your usual 85%.
whyItMatters: Explains why 'slumps' and 'hot streaks' often fade naturally.

definition: Counting and measuring every single member of a population, not just a sample.
example: A national count of every household every 10 years.
whyItMatters: Governments use census numbers to plan schools, roads, and hospitals.

definition: When outcomes happen without any predictable pattern or bias.
example: Shuffling a deck thoroughly or rolling a balanced die.
whyItMatters: True randomness is essential for fair games and encryption keys.

definition: The probability of getting a certain number of successes in repeated yes/no trials.
example: Counting how many free throws out of 10 a 70% shooter makes.
whyItMatters: Models coin flips, quality checks, and win-loss records.

definition: A grid table comparing counts across two categories at once.
example: Rows for Grade 5/6 and columns for Dog/Cat owners.
whyItMatters: Helps spot relationships between two survey questions.

definition: Fixing typos, duplicates, and missing entries before analyzing data.
example: Turning 'NYC', 'New York', and 'new york' into one consistent label.
whyItMatters: Garbage in, garbage out—clean data makes trustworthy results.

definition: Data that describes other data—like when, where, or how a file was made.
example: The date, camera model, and GPS spot saved inside a photo file.
whyItMatters: Helps organize millions of photos, songs, and web pages.

definition: Descriptive information using words or categories rather than numbers.
example: Eye color, favorite book, or weather ('sunny', 'rainy').
whyItMatters: Captures feelings, stories, and categories numbers miss.

definition: Information measured in numbers that you can count or add up.
example: Height in cm, age in years, or points scored.
whyItMatters: Lets you compute averages, charts, and exact comparisons.

definition: Numbers that can only take specific separate values, usually whole counts.
example: Number of siblings (0, 1, 2, 3—never 2.4).
whyItMatters: Helps choose the right chart type (bar chart vs. line).

definition: Measurements that can take any value along a smooth scale, including decimals.
example: Height (145.32 cm) or sprint time (12.48 seconds).
whyItMatters: Physical measurements like time, weight, and speed are continuous.

definition: When a model memorizes random noise in past data instead of learning the real pattern.
example: Studying only the exact order of practice answers and failing a slightly reworded test.
whyItMatters: A huge challenge in building smart AI systems.

definition: A standard test score used to compare different systems fairly.
example: Running the same 3D game scene on two graphics cards to compare FPS.
whyItMatters: Lets consumers compare phones, chips, and cars objectively.

definition: A visual grid that uses colors from cool to hot to show where values are highest.
example: Showing which spots on a soccer field a player runs on most.
whyItMatters: Makes dense tables and maps readable in one second.

definition: A starting measurement used as a reference point to measure future changes.
example: Recording your resting heart rate before starting a 6-week running plan.
whyItMatters: Without a baseline, you can't tell how much you improved.
